system_message:
You are generating a synthetic but clinically grounded
conversation for exactly one hospital admission.

Rules:
1. Use only facts supported by the provided admission context.
2. The discharge notes are the backbone of the hospital-course
   narrative. Use them first.
3. The ordered problem list should shape the main clinical focus.
4. Radiology, procedures, microbiology, and the previous-admission
   summary are supporting context, not a checklist.
5. Not every packet item needs to appear in the conversation.
6. Speakers must be exactly: Doctor and Patient.
7. Every conversation line must contain:
   - turn number
   - exact timestamp
   - speaker
   - text
8. Timestamps must be monotonically increasing and stay within the
   admission start and admission end times.
9. Keep the conversation medically plausible and understandable to
   a patient.
10. Use short natural exchanges, patient questions, clarifications,
    explanations, reassurance, and follow-up discussion.
11. Do not invent unsupported diagnoses, procedures, test findings,
    or outcomes.
12. Do not mention the dataset, packet, note types, or that the
    conversation is synthetic.
13. Generate the conversation first, then write the summary strictly from the generated conversation_lines.
14. Every claim in summary.summary_paragraph and every item in summary.problems must be explicitly supported by the conversation_lines.
15. Return output that exactly matches the required JSON schema.
task_message:
Generate one rich patient-doctor conversation for this admission and one admission summary.

Generation guidance:
- Approximate stay length: 4 day(s).
- Recommended turn range: 50-70 turns.
- Exact admission window: 2155-11-01 18:10:00 to 2155-11-04 19:22:00.
- Focus first on the discharge-note storyline and the core admission problems.
- Use radiology, procedures, and microbiology only as supporting detail when they help the story.
- Do not try to mention every packet item.
- Let the conversation unfold across admission, mid-course updates, and discharge planning.
- Prefer many short natural exchanges over a few long summary turns.
- The patient should ask questions, express concerns, seek clarification, and respond to updates throughout the stay.
- The doctor should explain results, treatment changes, progress, and follow-up in multiple conversational beats over time.
- You may paraphrase and add natural conversational glue, but do not invent unsupported diagnoses, procedures, findings, or outcomes.
- Generate the conversation first, then derive the final summary only from the conversation_lines you wrote.
- The final summary must contain admission start time, admission end time, one paragraph summary, and a list of problems.
- Final self-check before returning JSON: turn_number contiguous from 1; conversation_lines.time nondecreasing and inside the exact admission window; summary.admission_start and summary.admission_end copied exactly from the packet; no conversation line has empty text.

previous_admission_summary_used.summary_paragraph: The patient was admitted for an elective T3-4 and T6-7 transpedicular discectomy due to thoracic disc protrusions. Preoperatively, she received two units of platelets for mild thrombocytopenia. The surgery was performed successfully, and she tolerated it well, with stable neurological function postoperatively. On postoperative day two, she experienced a brief episode of hypoxemia, likely due to IV hydromorphone, which resolved after discontinuation. Her asthma, diabetes, and other comorbidities remained stable. She was discharged home with nursing and physical therapy support, ambulating at her baseline with a walker, and given detailed wound and medication instructions.
problems: Displacement of thoracic intervertebral disc without myelopathy
Large cell lymphoma, unspecified site, extranodal and solid organ sites
Diabetes mellitus without mention of complication, type II or unspecified type, not stated as uncontrolled
Other opiates and related narcotics causing adverse effects in therapeutic use

radiology_notes.text:
EXAMINATION:  CT OF THE ABDOMEN AND PELVIS.

INDICATION:  ___ year old woman with hx of lymphoma with prior colonic
involvement, s/p perforation, resection, colectomy in ___. Also with CVID. Pt
reports ___ hx of abdominal cramping, loose stool and nausea. Please further
evaluate.  // ___ year old woman with hx of lymphoma with prior colonic
involvement, s/p perforation, resection, colectomy in ___. Also with CVID. Pt
reports ___ hx of abdominal cramping, loose stool and nausea. Please further
evaluate.

TECHNIQUE:  MDCT axial images were acquired through abdomen and pelvis
following intravenous contrast administration with split bolus technique.
Coronal and sagittal reformations were performed and submitted to PACS for
review.

DOSE:  374 mGy-cm. 100 mL of Omnipaque intravenous contrast were administered.
Oral contrast was administered.

COMPARISON:  CT examination from ___.

FINDINGS:


Included views of the lung bases are clear.  There is no pericardial or
pleural effusion.  The heart size is normal.

The hepatic parenchyma demonstrates normal density.  No concerning hepatic
mass is detected.  Again seen is mild prominence of the CBD, measuring up to 8
mm in diameter, but tapering smoothly to the ampulla (series 6 image 22),
without obstructing mass or stone.  The gallbladder is normal.  The spleen is
enlarged, measuring up to 17.5 cm craniocaudally (series 6 image 28), slightly
enlarged since the ___ examination.

The pancreas, adrenal glands, kidneys, stomach, and intra-abdominal loops of
small bowel are within normal limits.

The patient is post left hemicolectomy with a left lower quadrant colostomy
(series 4 image 47).  There is no bowel obstruction or discrete

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi, I'm Dr. Lee. I’ll be taking care of you during your stay. Can you tell me what’s been going on?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Hi, thanks. I’ve had bad stomach cramps and diarrhea for about a month now. It started after I saw some sick kids and then got my IVIG infusion.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I see. And how frequent are the stools? Any blood or fever?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: A few times a day, liquid at first, but they’re starting to firm up. I had red stools once after red jello, but no more since. No fevers.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Okay, that helps. Given your history of lymphoma and immune deficiency, we want to be careful. We’ll run some tests.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve also been feeling dizzy when I stand up. Started a few days ago.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your blood pressure was low in clinic—94 over 55. That could explain the dizziness. We’ll monitor that.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my left shoulder’s been hurting for about a week. Was I supposed to get an X-ray before coming in?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, but it wasn’t done. We’ll order that tomorrow so we can check it out.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, thanks. I’m just worried it’s something serious with my lymphoma coming back.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I understand. But your symptoms are more likely due to an infection, especially since others around you were sick.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That makes sense. I’ve been trying to eat more carbs to firm up my stools, but it’s just made my blood sugar worse.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, we saw your HbA1c is 7%, so diabetes is under reasonable control. We’ll hold your metformin for now and use insulin as needed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Alright. What about my IVIG? I’m due for it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll give it during your stay. It’s important for your immune deficiency. We’ll also start antibiotics just in case.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m allergic to penicillin and sulfa drugs. Just so you know.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Noted. You already got cefepime and flagyl in clinic, which are safe for you. We’ll continue that.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. Your CT scan from yesterday didn’t show any new masses or bowel issues. Lymph nodes are stable, and your spleen is slightly larger but unchanged from before.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So nothing’s blocking or inflamed?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: No, the scan looks clear. That’s reassuring. Your shoulder X-ray is also normal—no fracture or arthritis.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So why does it hurt? Could it be lymphoma?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It’s possible, but unlikely. We’ll keep an eye on it. You may need an MRI later if it doesn’t improve.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, that’s a relief. How’s my blood work?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your white count is low—2.2—because of your immune condition. Hemoglobin is a bit low too, but stable. Platelets are okay.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Should I be worried about that?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Not acutely. Your levels are consistent with your history. We’ll keep monitoring.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re scheduling your colonoscopy for today. It’s mostly to rule out infection or inflammation since your symptoms haven’t fully resolved.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will they take biopsies?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, they’ll take a few samples. It might help us find a cause if it’s not just a virus.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my IVIG? Is that still happening?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, right after the colonoscopy. You’re getting your full dose.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The colonoscopy was unremarkable. The inside of your bowel looks healthy. No ulcers, masses, or active inflammation.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No sign of lymphoma?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: No visible signs. Biopsies are pending, but so far, nothing concerning. We also tested for C. diff and parasites—both negative.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And the CMV test?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: CMV came back negative. So it’s not that either.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So what’s causing this?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Most likely a lingering viral or bacterial gastroenteritis. Your immune deficiency makes it harder to clear infections quickly.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And the antibiotics will help?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, cipro and flagyl cover a broad range of bacteria. We’ll send you home with a full course.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What about the dizziness?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s improved, right? We think it was due to dehydration from diarrhea. Your blood pressure is still low but stable.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yeah, I feel less lightheaded now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good. We’ll keep an eye on it. Your ostomy site looks better too—less red than when you came in.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Morning. We’re planning to discharge you today. You’re feeling better, stools are firmer, and no new issues.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s great. What meds am I going home with?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: All your usual meds, plus cipro and flagyl for a week. Also, loperamide for diarrhea and dicyclomine for cramps if needed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And the Dilaudid? I know it’s limited.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, 18 tablets. Please discuss with your pain doctor about long-term use.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will do. Any follow-up tests?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes. We ordered a strongyloides IgG test—important for someone on IVIG. And please follow up on the colonoscopy biopsies.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my shoulder?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: If it doesn’t get better, your doctor may order an MRI. But for now, it’s likely musculoskeletal.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Got it. When should I call the doctor?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: If you develop fever, worsening pain, more diarrhea, or blood in stool—call right away.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my diabetes? Should I restart metformin?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, you can restart it tomorrow. Just monitor your sugars closely.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you, Dr. Lee. I feel much better.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. We’ll get your discharge papers ready. You should be out by noon.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Just a final check before you leave. Any new symptoms?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No, all good. Stomach feels better, and I’m not dizzy anymore.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Great. Remember to follow up with your primary doctor in a week.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. Thanks again for everything.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Take care. Feel better soon.

summary.summary_paragraph: The patient was admitted for evaluation of chronic abdominal pain and diarrhea lasting one month, in the context of multiple comorbidities including common variable immunodeficiency, large cell lymphoma in remission, and colostomy status. She also reported orthostatic dizziness and new left shoulder pain. Workup included a CT abdomen and pelvis showing stable retroperitoneal lymphadenopathy and no acute abdominal findings, a normal shoulder X-ray, and a colonoscopy with unremarkable findings and pending biopsies. Stool studies were negative for C. diff, parasites, and CMV. She was treated with intravenous antibiotics initiated in clinic and continued on ciprofloxacin and metronidazole, along with loperamide and dicyclomine for symptom control. Her symptoms improved during the hospitalization, dizziness resolved, and she was discharged home on a full course of oral antibiotics and updated symptom management medications. Follow-up was arranged for shoulder pain if persistent, strongyloides IgG results, and colonoscopy biopsies.
